system:
You read documents filed on a United States court docket, OCR'd to markdown, for
a research dataset of contract clauses.

An INSTRUMENT is a document whose text the parties negotiated and by which they
bound each other: a contract, agreement, policy, lease, deed, guaranty, note,
plan, bylaws, handbook, amendment, or similar. Hallmarks: recitals, defined
terms, numbered operative sections, an execution or signature block.

A FILING is a document made for the court: complaint, answer, motion, brief,
memorandum, order, affidavit, declaration, notice, docket sheet, certificate of
service, civil cover sheet.

THE DECISIVE RULE. A filing that **attaches** an instrument counts — report the
instrument's own boundaries, not the filing's. A filing that merely **quotes** an
instrument does not count at all: a brief reproducing three sentences of an
agreement is a filing, and the file contains no instrument.

WHAT IS NOT AN INSTRUMENT, even when signed or filled in: a blank or fill-in
form; an agency certificate or registration; an exhibit index; a declarations
page or coverage-summary table; a schedule of rates or fees standing alone; an
invoice, receipt or statement of account. These record or summarise; the parties
did not negotiate their text.

WHAT IS NOT A PROVISION: a heading on its own; a title page; a table of
contents; a signature, notary or attestation block; an exhibit index. A
provision states an obligation, right, grant, limitation, condition or
definition. Give the range of the operative text, including its heading.

LIST EVERY SUBSTANTIVE PROVISION, in document order. Do not skip any. Do not
judge whether a provision is well or badly drafted. Do not rank them.

The file is given to you with a line number and a `│` at the start of every line.
Line numbers are not part of the text; they are how you point at it.

OCR REPAIR. For each provision you must also give its text. Copy it verbatim
from the lines you named, then repair only what the scanner broke: words split
across a line break, words run together, `l`/`1` and `O`/`0` confusions, stray
table pipes and cell debris, page numbers and Bates stamps sitting inside the
text. Do not paraphrase, modernise, reorder, summarise, or drop anything. Never
change a number, an amount, a date, or a cross-reference. Never add or remove a
word — a repair that deletes `not` inverts the clause. If a passage is too
damaged to repair honestly, copy it as it stands.

Add nothing of your own: no `[struck through: ...]`, no `[sic]`, no
`[illegible]`, no explanatory brackets of any kind. Executed contracts are often
marked up by hand, and the OCR shows deleted wording as `~~struck~~`. Reproduce
those words as plain text, in place, and say what you saw in the repairs
sentence instead.

FILE: Exhibit Statement of Undisputed Facts in Support of Motion for Summary Judgment.md
FILED IN: 68 F.Supp.3d 817

    1│
    2│
    3│# **IN THE UNITED STATES DISTRICT COURT FOR THE WESTERN DISTRICT OF TENNESSEE WESTERN DIVISION**
    4│
    5│---
    6│
    7│**MCMAHAN JETS, LLC,**
    8│
    9│**Plaintiff,**
   10│
   11│**v.**
   12│
   13│**ROADLINK TRANSPORTATION INC.,  
   14│RIZO JET AVIATION SERVICES, LLC,  
   15│and JOHN/JANE DOE,**
   16│
   17│**Defendants.**
   18│
   19│---
   20│
   21│**Case No. 2:11-cv-03112-WGY-tmp**
   22│
   23│## --- **STATEMENT OF UNDISPUTED MATERIAL FACTS OF ROADLINK TRANSPORTATION, INC. IN SUPPORT OF MOTION FOR SUMMARY JUDGMENT** ---
   24│
   25│Defendant, Roadlink Transportation Inc., n/k/a Flying J Transportation Canada Inc. (“Roadlink”), pursuant to Federal Rule of Civil Procedure 56 and Local Rule 56.1(a), respectfully submits this Statement of Undisputed Material Facts in support of its Motion for Summary Judgment as to all claims asserted against it by Plaintiff, McMahan Jets, LLC (“McMahan Jets”):
   26│
   27│1. McMahan Jets is a Mississippi limited liability company, with its principal place of business in Hattiesburg, Mississippi. (Compl. (Doc. 1-2) ¶ 1.)
   28│
   29│2. It was “established for the purpose of renting, leasing, and selling aircraft,” and its owner and President is Dr. Lynn McMahan. (*Id.* ¶ 7.)
   30│
   31│3. In early January of 2008, Dr. McMahan and his wife, Marty McMahan, traveled to Sierra Industries, Inc. (“Sierra”) in Uvalde, Texas, to inspect a different airplane for possible
   32│
   33│purchase. (Deposition of Lynn Bryce McMahan, Oct. 18, 2013 (“McMahan Dep.”), excerpts attached hereto as **Exhibit A**, at 56:21-57:23.)
   34│
   35│4. Sierra is in the business of, *inter alia*, restoring and modifying Cessna Citations. (*Id.* at 57:7-16.)
   36│
   37│5. The McMahans traveled to Uvalde with Paul Daughtrey of Diamond Aviation, LLC, whom McMahan Jets had hired to be its pilot. (*Id.* at 61:11-17.)
   38│
   39│6. While in Uvalde, Dr. and Mrs. McMahan saw the Aircraft that is the subject of this action. (*Id.* at 58:21-59:23.)
   40│
   41│7. Sierra was performing work on the Aircraft, and the Sierra agent showed it to the McMahans as an example of the modifications that could be done to a Citation. (*Id.* at 62:1-14, 62:23-63:7.)
   42│
   43│8. Though the McMahans were interested in the Aircraft, Sierra did not have the Aircraft listed for sale, so the McMahans instructed Mr. Daughtrey to stay in Texas to find out more information about the Aircraft. (*Id.* at 59:13-23, 61:11-62:14.)
   44│
   45│9. At that time, the Aircraft was owned by Roadlink. (Deposition of Ellen Joan Toscano, Oct. 8, 2013 (“Toscano Dep.”), excerpts attached hereto as **Exhibit B**, at 39:12-15, 75:2-14.)
   46│
   47│10. Title to the Aircraft was transferred to Roadlink in December of 2007 by Flying J Inc., Roadlink’s parent corporation, prior to the McMahan’s trip to Texas. (Toscano Dep. 37:14-38:25; Dep. Ex. 6, attached hereto as **Exhibit C**.)
   48│
   49│11. Roadlink is a Utah corporation, with its principal place of business in Ogden, Utah. (Declaration of Chris J. Malan (“Malan Decl.”) (Doc. 20-2), at ¶ 2.)
   50│
   51│12. Roadlink is now known as Flying J Transportation Canada, Inc., having changed its name on September 22, 2008. (Declaration of Robert Payne (Doc. 60-3), at ¶ 7.)
   52│
   53│13. Roadlink's business is the acquisition and maintenance of airplanes and the ownership, operation, and lease of semi-trucks and trailers used in Canadian-related petroleum product hauling. (Malan Decl. ¶ 20.)
   54│
   55│14. When the McMahans saw the Aircraft, Roadlink had not listed the Aircraft for sale, nor had it contracted with a broker at that point. (Toscano Dep. 25:18-26:1.)
   56│
   57│15. Soon after the McMahans' trip to Texas, Manuel Rizo of Rizo Jet Aviation Services, LLC ("Rizo") contacted Cliff Gottschalk, Roadlink's Director of Maintenance, about the Aircraft. (Deposition of Clifford Gottschalk, Oct. 9, 2013 ("Gottschalk Dep."), excerpts attached hereto as **Exhibit D**, at 139:11-21.)
   58│
   59│16. Rizo is a Texas limited liability company, with its principal place of business in Hondo, Texas. (Compl. ¶ 3.)
   60│
   61│17. Mr. Gottschalk was previously acquainted with Mr. Rizo because Mr. Rizo had worked at Sierra. (Gottschalk Dep. 104:16-105:10.)
   62│
   63│18. Mr. Rizo informed Mr. Gottschalk that he had been contacted by Mr. Daughtrey, who told Mr. Rizo that the McMahans had seen the Aircraft while in Texas and were interested in purchasing it. (*Id.* at 139:19-141:5.)
   64│
   65│19. Although Roadlink had not listed the Aircraft for sale, it was amenable to selling it. (*Id.* at 139:19-140:5.)
   66│
   67│20. Roadlink did not want to pay Rizo a large broker's fee for the sale, so it was agreed that Roadlink would sell the Aircraft to Rizo, which would then sell it to McMahan Jets. (*Id.* at 139:19-141:5.)
   68│
   69│21. Because Rizo was not registered to transfer aircraft on the International Registry, however, the Aircraft was ultimately transferred directly from Roadlink to McMahan Jets. (Toscano Dep. 80:7-21.)
   70│
   71│22. Between January 3 and January 15, 2008, Mr. Daughtrey and Mr. Rizo worked out the terms of the transactions. (McMahan Dep. 79:18-80:13, 82:6-24.)
   72│
   73│23. At some point during that time, Mr. Daughtrey informed Dr. McMahan that the Aircraft was owned by Roadlink, which Dr. McMahan understood to be an entity related to Flying J, Inc., and that Rizo was its broker. (*Id.* at 77:23-78:16.)
   74│
   75│24. Mr. Daughtrey provided Dr. McMahan with an appraisal from Rizo indicating that the Aircraft had undergone a recent Phase 1-5 inspection. (*Id.* at 80:18-81:17.)
   76│
   77│25. A “Phase 1-5 inspection” is actually a series of inspections, Phase 1 through Phase 5, on a Cessna Citation as laid out in Cessna’s maintenance manuals and maintenance program. (Gottschalk Dep. 64:19-65:14; Deposition of William F. Haberstock, Oct. 8, 2013 (“Haberstock Dep.”), excerpts attached hereto as **Exhibit E**, at 32:2-12.)
   78│
   79│26. The Phase 5 inspection is structural and requires inspection of “the deeper areas” of the aircraft. (Haberstock Dep. 30:9-13.)
   80│
   81│27. Phase 5 inspections are required every three years or 1,200 hours and involve stripping down the interior of the aircraft. (Gottschalk Dep. 32:7-9, 193:11-20.)
   82│
   83│28. Dr. McMahan does not recall communicating with Mr. Rizo during this time period and suspects that all of his communications related to the transaction were with Mr. Daughtrey. (McMahan Dep. 82:6-24.)
   84│
   85│29. On January 10, 2008, McMahan Jets and Rizo executed an Aircraft Purchase Agreement (the “McMahan-Rizo Agreement”). (McMahan-Rizo Agreement (Doc. 60-5), and attached hereto as **Exhibit F.**)
   86│
   87│30. The McMahan-Rizo Agreement provides for a purchase price of \$2,100,000. (*Id.* § 2.1.)
   88│
   89│31. The Agreement provides that Aero-Space Reports, Inc. (“Aero-Space”), in Oklahoma City, would serve as “closing/escrow agent for this sale.” (*Id.* § 2.3.)
   90│
   91│32. Upon execution of the agreement, McMahan Jets was to pay a deposit of \$100,000 to be held in escrow by Aero-Space. (*Id.* § 2.1(a).)
   92│
   93│33. The balance of \$2,000,000 was to be wired by McMahan Jets to Aero-Space “prior to closing.” (*Id.* § 2.3.)
   94│
   95│34. The McMahan-Rizo Agreement provides that McMahan Jets would conduct a pre-purchase inspection, to be performed by X-Air Flight Support (“X-Air”) in Texas. (*Id.* § 3.1.)
   96│
   97│35. Dr. McMahan has acknowledged that he hired X-Air to do the inspection. (McMahan Dep. 124:18-24.)
   98│
   99│36. Based on that inspection, McMahan Jets was to provide the seller with a list of “Airworthy discrepancies,” and the seller had the option of paying to repair them, reducing the purchase price, or terminating the agreement. (McMahan-Rizo Agreement § 3.2.)
  100│
  101│37. After the inspection, McMahan Jets was to “sign a Technical Acceptance Letter (Exhibit B).” (*Id.* § 3.3; *see also id.* § 3.4 (“Purchaser will accept or reject Aircraft and will advise Seller in writing in the form of Exhibit B to this Agreement . . . upon satisfaction of the Pre-Purchase Inspection . . . of his decision to accept or reject the Aircraft.”).)
  102│
  103│38. The Technical Acceptance Letter attached to the agreement as Exhibit B identifies Mr. Rizo as the Seller, Roadlink as the Owner, and McMahan Jets as the Purchaser. (*Id.* at Roadlink 00073.)
  104│
  105│39. The McMahan-Rizo Agreement provided that the Aircraft would be delivered in Memphis, Tennessee (*Id.* § 5.)
  106│
  107│40. McMahan Jets chose Memphis as the location for delivery to take advantage of a fly-away rule that allowed McMahan Jets to avoid paying sales tax on the transaction. (McMahan Dep. 35:9-36:14.)
  108│
  109│41. McMahan Jets agreed that the “Aircraft will be delivered ‘AS IS WHERE IS,’” subject to the satisfaction of any discrepancies identified by McMahan Jets following the pre-purchase inspection. (McMahan-Rizo Agreement § 6.1.)
  110│
  111│42. “Risk of loss or damage to the Aircraft shall pass to Purchaser upon transfer of the funds of the Purchase Price and the passage of title by Bill of Sale to Purchaser.” (*Id.* § 4.3.)
  112│
  113│43. Section 6.3 provides:
  114│
  115│The Aircraft is being sold without any warranty from Seller or any original equipment from the manufacturer of the Aircraft, Cessna Aircraft Corporation. Seller acknowledges that Purchaser has had full opportunity to inspect the Aircraft and to have such tests and inspections performed by third parties as the Purchaser deems necessary or desirable, in Purchaser’s sole discretion. Purchase is at Purchaser’s sole discretion, and Purchaser understands that this is a final sale. Seller shall have no liability by reason of the manufacture or sale of the Aircraft or of the operation, use, maintenance or storage of the Aircraft, whether on the basis of breach of warranty, strict liability, negligence or otherwise. In no event shall Seller be liable for general, special and consequential or incidental damages relating to property damage or economic loss including, without limitation, damages for the loss of use or loss of profits. Purchaser understands, agrees and accepts that Seller is selling the Aircraft and it’s [sic] equipment “AS IS, WHERE IS” with all faults and/or deficiencies, provided however, that Seller, has satisfied the condition of Section 3.2, if necessary. NO WARRANTIES OF ANY TYPE WHETHER OF MERCHANTABILITY, FITNESS FOR A PARTICULAR PURPOSE OR OTHERWISE, EXPRESS OR IMPLIED, IN FACT OR BY LAW,
  116│
  117│IS OR SHALL BE APPLICABLE TO THE Aircraft, THE CONDITION OF THE AIRCRAFT OR ITS PARTS OR ACCESSORIES.
  118│
  119│(*Id.* § 6.3.)
  120│
  121│44. On January 10, 2008, McMahan Jets and Rizo executed Escrow Instructions, providing that the parties agreed to use Aero-Space “as closing agent for this transaction.” (Escrow Instructions, Roadlink 00063, attached hereto as **Exhibit G.**)
  122│
  123│45. Roadlink and Rizo executed identical Escrow Instructions. (Escrow Instructions, Roadlink 00050, attached hereto as **Exhibit H.**)
  124│
  125│46. McMahan wired a \$100,000 deposit from its bank account in Mississippi to Aero-Space in Oklahoma City on January 10, 2008. (Wire Transfer Notices, Aero Space 000027-43, attached hereto as **Exhibit I.**, at Aero Space 000027.)
  126│
  127│47. Roadlink sent Aero-Space a signed, undated Aircraft Bill of Sale, designating the transfer of the Aircraft from Roadlink to McMahan Jets, and a signed, undated Release, demonstrating that the Aircraft was free from liens. (Aircraft Bill of Sale, Roadlink 00119, attached hereto as **Exhibit J.**; Release, MJ0090, attached hereto as **Exhibit K.**)
  128│
  129│48. Aero-Space held these documents in escrow until closing. (Toscano Dep. 29:18-30:5, 47:5-19, 57:7-24.)
  130│
  131│49. On or about January 15, 2008, the McMahans met Mr. Daughtrey in Hondo, Texas, where X-Air was performing the pre-purchase inspection of the Aircraft, to conduct the test flight and visual inspection of the Aircraft. (McMahan Dep. 83:24-84:19.)
  132│
  133│50. Though Mr. Gottschalk encouraged Mr. Daughtrey to have a Phase 1-5 inspection performed, which is more costly, McMahan Jets did not do so. (Gottschalk Dep. 108:7-25.)
  134│
  135│51. McMahan Jets paid X-Air \$5,000 to conduct the pre-purchase inspection. (McMahan Dep. 91:17-92:13; Invoice, MJ0043, attached hereto as **Exhibit L.**)
  136│
  137│52. McMahan Jets compensated Mr. Daughtrey approximately \$17,000 for his services related to the acquisition of the Aircraft. (McMahan Dep. 68:1-4.)
  138│
  139│53. As part of the pre-purchase inspection, X-Air reviewed the Aircraft's logbooks. (Gottschalk Dep. 107:8-24; McMahan Dep. 102:19-22.)
  140│
  141│54. The logbooks contain, *inter alia*, entries regarding an inspection by CR Aviation, Inc. in February of 2000, a Phase 1-5 inspection by Sierra on September 10, 2001, another Phase 1-5 inspection by Mr. Gottschalk on October 22, 2004, and a final Phase 1-5 inspection by Mr. Gottschalk on October 21, 2007, a few months before the transaction giving rise to this lawsuit. (Dep. Ex. 31, attached hereto as **Exhibit M**; Dep. Ex. 36, attached hereto as **Exhibit N**; Dep. Ex. 44, attached hereto as **Exhibit O**; Dep. Ex. 110, attached hereto as **Exhibit P**.)
  142│
  143│55. The Phase 1-5 inspections by Mr. Gottschalk identify him as an employee of "Flying J, Inc." (Dep. Exs. 31, 110.)
  144│
  145│56. On January 16, 2008, Roadlink and Rizo executed an Aircraft Purchase Agreement similar to that entered into by Rizo and McMahan, but identifying Rizo as the Purchaser and Roadlink as the Seller (the "Roadlink-Rizo Agreement"). (Doc. 60-6.)
  146│
  147│57. The purchase price to be paid by Rizo to Roadlink was \$1,950,000—as opposed to the \$2.1 million purchase price listed in the McMahan-Rizo Agreement. (*Id.* § 2.1; McMahan-Rizo Agreement § 2.1.)
  148│
  149│58. The Roadlink-Rizo Agreement contains a Texas choice-of-venue provision, whereas the McMahan-Rizo Agreement contains a Mississippi choice-of-venue provision. (Roadlink-Rizo Agreement § 8.6; McMahan-Rizo Agreement § 8.6.)
  150│
  151│59. At some point in time, Mr. Daughtrey and Mr. Rizo entered into a confidential agreement whereby they would split the difference between the price McMahan Jets agreed to
  152│
  153│pay for the Aircraft, \$2.1 million, and the price Roadlink agreed to accept, \$1.95 million.
  154│
  155│(McMahan Dep. 103:14-104:14; Fax from P. Daughtrey, Aero Space 000058, attached hereto as **Exhibit Q**; Agreement, Aero Space 000122-24, attached hereto as **Exhibit R**; Letter, Aero Space 000164, attached hereto as **Exhibit S**.)
  156│
  157│60. Neither McMahan Jets nor Roadlink was aware of this arrangement or of the price the other had agreed to, until it was revealed during discovery in this matter. (Gottschalk Dep. 160:4-9; McMahan Dep. 103:2-104:19, 124:18-125:3, 132:6-10.)
  158│
  159│61. Mr. Daughtrey and Mr. Rizo communicated the arrangement to Aero-Space, which prepared two sets of closing instructions—one for McMahan Jets showing receipt and disbursement of \$2.1 million, and one for Roadlink showing receipt and disbursement of \$1.95 million. (Dep. Ex. 20, attached hereto as **Exhibit T**; Dep. Ex. 25, attached hereto as **Exhibit U**.)
  160│
  161│62. Neither set of instructions revealed that Aero-Space was going to disburse the \$150,000 difference to Mr. Daughtrey and Mr. Rizo. (Dep. Exs. 20, 25.)
  162│
  163│63. Roadlink was not aware that McMahan Jets was paying \$2.1 million for the Aircraft. (Gottschalk Dep. 161:3-23; Toscano Dep. 93:20-94:1, 104:10-25.)
  164│
  165│64. On January 21, 2008, X-Air provided a Prepurchase Report to McMahan Jets. (Dep. Ex. 39, attached hereto as **Exhibit V**.)
  166│
  167│65. Upon receiving the report, McMahan Jets executed the Technical Acceptance Letter on January 23, 2008. (McMahan-Rizo Agreement, at Roadlink 00073.)
  168│
  169│66. McMahan Jets identified no discrepancies and stated that “the Aircraft is satisfactory and is hereby accepted in accordance with the terms of the Agreement.” (*Id.*)
  170│
  171│67. The same day, McMahan Jets withdrew \$2,002,440 from its bank account in Mississippi and wired the funds directly to Aero-Space in Oklahoma. (Wire Transfer Notices, at Aero Space 000028.)
  172│
  173│68. On January 24, 2008, Dr. McMahan and Mr. Daughtrey traveled to Memphis from Mississippi. (McMahan Dep. 156:13-15; Gottschalk Dep. 172:1-9.)
  174│
  175│69. The same day, Mr. Gottschalk, Mr. Rizo, and two of Roadlink's pilots flew to Memphis in the Aircraft and delivered it to McMahan Jets. (Gottschalk Dep. 149:13-14.)
  176│
  177│70. After delivery, McMahan Jets transmitted via facsimile from Mississippi to Aero-Space in Oklahoma City a signed document entitled Authorization to Close. (Authorization to Close, MJ0024, attached hereto as **Exhibit W**.)
  178│
  179│71. Aero-Space filed the original Bill of Sale with the FAA on January 24, 2008, at 2:27 p.m. (See Aero-Space Letter, MJ0104, attached hereto as **Exhibit X**.)
  180│
  181│72. Aero-Space then released the funds from escrow in Oklahoma, disbursing \$1.95 million as Roadlink had approved, and disbursing the remaining \$150,000 pursuant to Mr. Daughtrey and Mr. Rizo's secret agreement, with \$86,100 going to Diamond Aviation and \$63,900 to Rizo, in addition to the \$25,000 commission Roadlink had agreed to pay Rizo. (Settlement Sheet, Aero Space 000026, attached hereto as **Exhibit Y**; Wire Transfer Notices, at 000028-43; Dep. Ex. 20)
  182│
  183│73. McMahan Jets operated the Aircraft for the next 22 months for business and personal use. (McMahan Dep. 52:19-53:12.)
  184│
  185│74. Dr. McMahan loved the Aircraft and had no problems with it. (*Id.* at 54:21-56:4.)
  186│
  187│75. In November of 2009, McMahan Jets took the Aircraft to Orlando, Florida, where the Cessna Service Center performed a mandatory Phase 1-5 inspection and subsequently
  188│
  189│informed McMahan Jets of the existence of the holes in the carry-through spar. (*Id.* at 52:22-53:3, 130:12-24.)
  190│
  191│76. The forward carry-through spar is “the wing spar in the center section within the fuselage, and it may extend a little beyond the edges of the fuselage, and it is the attach point for the wings.” (Haberstock Dep. 19:25-20:17.)
  192│
  193│77. It is a major structural component of an aircraft. (*Id.*)
  194│
  195│78. Cessna ultimately concluded that the Aircraft was not airworthy due to the existence of the holes in the spar. (Letter, MJ0140-41, attached hereto as **Exhibit Z**.)
  196│
  197│79. Cessna provided a quote to replace the spar for \$463,000.00, which Cessna said was the required repair. (*Id.*)
  198│
  199│80. Roadlink did not drill the holes in the spar; they were present when Roadlink’s predecessor acquired the Aircraft from the previous Venezuelan owner in in February of 2000. (Gottschalk Dep. 174:13-20, 175:25-176:9.)
  200│
  201│81. Mr. Gottschalk first learned of the holes in February of 2000, when CR Aviation performed an inspection that included stripping down the interior. (*Id.* at 94:3-19, 176:20-177:14, 193:3-20.)
  202│
  203│82. Despite the presence of the holes in the spar, CR Aviation issued an airworthiness certificate. (*Id.* at 176:4-19, 178:15-179:21, 180:1-12, 181:8-182:1; Dep. Ex. 44; Dep. Ex. 45, attached hereto as **Exhibit AA**; Dep. Ex. 46, attached hereto as **Exhibit BB**.)
  204│
  205│83. On September 10, 2001, Sierra performed a Phase 1-5 inspection on the Aircraft. (Gottschalk Dep. 177:15-20; Dep. Ex 36.)
  206│
  207│84. Sierra informed Mr. Gottschalk that the holes in the spar were not a problem, and Sierra also issued an airworthiness certificate. (Gottschalk Dep. 178:1-14, 182:7-25; Dep. Ex. 47, attached hereto as **Exhibit CC**.)
  208│
  209│85. When Mr. Gottschalk performed the next Phase 1-5 inspection on October 22, 2004, he listed the presence of the holes on a discrepancy form, noting that they had been “previously ok’d by CR Aviation and Sierra – N/A.” (Gottschalk Dep. 106:12-18, 184:5-23; Dep. Ex. 30, attached hereto as **Exhibit DD**.)
  210│
  211│86. Consistent with industry practice, Mr. Gottschalk did not put the discrepancy forms in the logbooks, and, therefore, these forms were not provided to X-Air or McMahan Jets. (Haberstock Dep. 82:3-21.)
  212│
  213│87. Had McMahan Jets commissioned a Phase 1-5 inspection of the Aircraft during the pre-purchase inspection (as it was permitted and encouraged to do), that inspection would have revealed the existence of the holes in the spar. (Deposition of John B. Bell, Oct. 16, 2013 (“Bell Dep.”), excerpts attached hereto as **Exhibit EE**, at 45:14-19; Haberstock Dep. 34:19-35:1.)
  214│
  215│88. Mr. Gottschalk believed that the holes did not affect the airworthiness of the Aircraft. (Gottschalk Dep. 125:24-126:6, 153:15-24.)
  216│
  217│89. That opinion was based on his experience with aircrafts, as well as on the opinions he received from CR Aviation and Sierra. (*Id.* at 106:12-18, 123:16-23, 125:24-126:16, 153:15-154:3, 181:8-182:22, 192:11-17.)
  218│
  219│90. Mr. Gottschalk personally flew in the Aircraft for approximately 250 hours over eight years. (*Id.* at 185:2-186:2.)
  220│
  221│91. The corporate officers of Roadlink and Flying J flew in the Aircraft frequently, including the top management of the companies and their families. (*Id.*)
  222│
  223│92. Mr. Gottschalk would not have flown in the Aircraft, and he would not have allowed his employers or their families to fly in the Aircraft, if he had any belief that it was not airworthy. (*Id.*)
  224│
  225│93. A “Mandatory Service Bulletin” is a post-manufacture change in operation and/or inspection of an aircraft or aircraft part that is issued by the original equipment manufacturer (or “OEM”). (Haberstock Dep. 41:17-42:8.)
  226│
  227│94. There were no Airworthiness Directives or Mandatory Service Bulletins that had not been complied with in this case. (Haberstock Expert Report, Dep. Ex. 27, attached hereto as **Exhibit FF**, at 2.)
  228│
  229│95. Exhibit B to the agreement, the “Technical Acceptance Letter,” which McMahan Jets executed to provide:
  230│
  231│No items were discovered during the Inspection that cause the Aircraft to be out of compliance with the Aircraft condition required by the Agreement, and the Aircraft is satisfactory and is hereby accepted in accordance with the terms of the Agreement.
  232│
  233│(McMahan-Rizo Agreement, at Roadlink 00073.)
  234│
  235│96. Dr. McMahan does not recall speaking to any employee or agent of Roadlink about the condition of the Aircraft, and he is not aware of any such statements made by Roadlink to any of McMahan Jets’ employees or agents. (McMahan Dep. 82:6-24, 88:24-89:11, 99:3-15 (“Did Mr. Rizo ever at any time discuss the condition of the plane with you? A. I have no memory of it.”), 119:10-18, 120:3-8, 121:7-14, 141:15-143:20.)
  236│
